claims.text: Untreated Q235 steel has a native, in situ-formed oxide film in its pre-exposure state.
Mild electrochemical pre-conditioning can control the thickness and composition of the native oxide film on Q235 steel.
Electrochemical pre-conditioning will make the Q235 oxide film more uniform and chemically rich.
The modified Q235 oxide film may contain TiO2 and Nb2O5.
TiO2 and Nb2O5 enhance corrosion resistance by acting as barriers to chloride ingress.
A robust and uniform oxide film improves passivation by reducing defects and inhibiting aggressive-ion penetration.
At room temperature, the controlled oxide film maintains an effective corrosion barrier on Q235 steel.
At room temperature, pre-conditioning delays corrosion initiation relative to untreated Q235 steel.
At room temperature, pre-conditioned samples will have lower corrosion current density than untreated samples.
At room temperature, pre-conditioned samples will have higher polarization resistance than untreated samples.
Elevated temperature generates thermal stresses that cause microstructural degradation or delamination of the oxide film.
Thermally induced film degradation facilitates corrosion initiation.
At elevated temperature, the protective advantage of pre-conditioning will diminish relative to its room-temperature advantage.
At elevated temperature, pre-conditioned samples will exhibit corrosion rates similar to or greater than untreated samples because of film degradation.
Cold rolling and precipitation-hardening treatments can increase corrosion resistance in a Ti80-Nb10-Mo5-Sn5 alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls the material 'pre-exposed,' whereas the initial-state field defines it as pre-exposure and untreated.
The mediator invokes TiO2 and Nb2O5, but neither the Q235 composition nor the electrochemical treatment specifies a source or deposition step for Ti or Nb.
